title: Scouting Design, Sampling and Plant-Health Records

content.overview: Scouting is a measurement system. Reliable plant-health decisions require consistent routes, sampling units, observation categories and location records so changes in pest or disease pressure can be separated from memory and anecdote.

vocabulary.definition: The proportion or count of sampled units showing a pest, disease or symptom.
The degree of damage or symptom expression on an affected unit.
A deliberately monitored site likely to reveal early entry or recurring risk.

sections.title: Consistency creates comparable data
sections.body: Use repeatable zones, plant counts and observation methods. Changing the scouting route each time makes trends harder to interpret.

sections.title: Map where problems occur
sections.body: Root disease, foliar disease and arthropod pressure can cluster with propagation batches, airflow, irrigation or traffic patterns. Location and batch IDs turn observations into traceable evidence.

sections.title: Absence of evidence depends on sampling effort
sections.body: A clean-looking room is not proof of zero pressure. Record how many plants or traps were checked and where they were located.

workedExamples: Three mites on one edge plant have a different management meaning from three mites found across three distant zones.
Repeated root symptoms in one propagation batch suggest tracing source material and irrigation history rather than treating the entire facility as one unit.
commonMistakes: Changing routes and sample size without noting it.
Failing to connect findings to room, bench, batch or cultivar.
content.practicalApplication: Define a weekly scouting map with fixed zones, a minimum sample count, trap IDs where used, severity categories and escalation rules. Preserve negative as well as positive observations.
content.summary: Advanced scouting turns plant-health observations into comparable spatial and temporal data.
